title: Doob Gaya Hum, Duba Diya Hum Ne

cover.alt: Doob Gaya Hum, Duba Diya Hum Ne

sections.text:
Water has always been a mirror — it reflects not just light but longing, memory, and the human desire to belong. This series documents the slow submergence of familiar landscapes and the communities tied to them.

The title, translating loosely as 'We drowned, and we drowned it,' carries within it both lament and complicity — an acknowledgment that we are both victim and agent of loss.
These photographs were made at the edge of things — where land meets water, where the known world ends. They ask what we choose to preserve, what we allow to dissolve, and who gets to decide.
Exhibited at Alliance Française Gallery, Ahmedabad, 2013.

title: Trespass – Missing Interiors
venue: Corner Stone Gallery, Hope University, Manchester

sections.text:
Human beings are supposed to be social animals — we live together and share things that are commonly used. But in reality, there is a tendency to demarcate our spaces. In a larger spectrum, the division of countries and states is evidence of it.

When one takes a closer look, it is evident that beyond political convenience there is an underlying reason: personalising and owning.

Humans within society also mark their territory. People customise their spaces to demarcate and declare. When a country conquers another, they put up flags — signs to prove the presence of the new owner. Sometimes the invasion happens very slowly, invisible at a glance. The change is only visible after a period of time.

This project looks at changes in personal spaces — from a bachelor's life to the life of a family person. All the personal spaces that were the property of a single man slowly taken over by children as they came in. It is a continuous process. The transformation happens very slowly.

At one moment the photographer looks back and documents the changes. All the spaces have been trespassed — without even knowing it. The marks they left behind are the evidence.

This is a series done over a period of four years.

Objects carry memory. A found thing is rarely without history — it arrived somewhere by chance, by loss, by the slow drift of time.

This series explores the intimate relationship between people and the objects they leave behind, accumulate, and sometimes rediscover.
In the spaces between possession and loss, we find the residue of living — accumulated not by intention, but by the passage of time itself.
Every object is also a portrait — of the person who owned it, the moment they let it go.

title: Roti Kapada Makan
venue: Ojas Art Gallery, New Delhi · Curated by Anubhav Nath

sections.text:
Food, clothing, shelter — the three essentials of human existence, reduced to a political slogan, but lived as something far more complex.

This body of work looks at how these basics are negotiated across class, community, and geography in contemporary India.
Part of a group exhibition curated by Anubhav Nath at Ojas Art Gallery, New Delhi, 2012.

A memorial is not always stone and marble. Sometimes it is light falling across an ordinary afternoon.

This series is an act of witnessing — photographs made in the presence of grief, of love that has no object left to hold onto.
To photograph grief is not to exploit it — it is to say: this happened, this mattered, this person existed.
